query: What AIS-based metrics and diagnostics most reliably detect cross-border effort displacement, reflagging, or distant-water fishing responses to FTAs?

response.query: What AIS-based metrics and diagnostics most reliably detect cross-border effort displacement, reflagging, or distant-water fishing responses to FTAs?
response.answer: AIS-based metrics like apparent fishing effort and vessel movement patterns reliably detect cross-border effort displacement, reflagging, or distant-water fishing responses to FTAs. These metrics highlight changes in vessel activity and location.

results.title: Apparent fishing effort (AIS) - Global Fishing Watch
results.content: # Apparent fishing effort (AIS). Global Fishing Watch collects and analyzes AIS data transmitted by vessels to understand global vessel activity. AIS data includes a vessel’s identity, location, speed, direction and more, collected through a global network of satellite and terrestrial receivers. Global Fishing Watch processes billions of AIS messages daily, focusing on vessels likely to be fishing based on their movement patterns and registry information. To produce a global dataset of fishing activity predictions—tracking positions interpreted as indicative of fishing—our general fishing model must operate across diverse fisheries, each with varying definitions of what constitutes “fishing.” As a result, the training data used to build the model, and thus the predicted fishing activity, encompass a range of fishing-related behaviors, including searching, setting gear, hauling and gear soaking. * **Support enforcement and compliance:** AIS data helps identify suspicious vessel behavior, such as potential fishing near MPAs. This aids authorities in prioritizing patrols and investigations. * **Inform fisheries management and spatial planning:** AIS-derived apparent fishing effort can be layered with ecological and jurisdictional data to support zoning decisions, policy development and ecosystem-based management. Many small-scale or artisanal vessels do not carry AIS and subsequently are not captured in the AIS-based apparent fishing effort layer. * **Interpretation over time:** Increases or decreases in apparent activity could reflect changing AIS usage, changing access to terrestrial stations or dynamic AIS, or reception quality rather than actual changes in fishing behavior. * **False positives:** AIS-based models identify fishing based on movement patterns. All vessel data are freely available through the Global Fishing Watch data portal at To learn more, read the supplementary materials of the Global Fishing Watch AIS-based fishing activity paper. Data on apparent fishing effort is available through several Global Fishing Watch tools:. * Global Fishing Watch Map: View near real-time apparent fishing effort derived from AIS data. * APIs and packages: Access apparent fishing effort data programmatically through the Global Fishing Watch 4Wings API, as well as the gfwr package for R users and the Global Fishing Watch Python package. This data differs from the data available in the Map and APIs. Each tool offers access to different components of the apparent fishing effort dataset.

results.title: Downloadable Fishing Effort Data | Global Fishing Watch
results.content:
Title: Downloadable Fishing Effort Data | Global Fishing Watch
Global Fishing Watch’s flagship dataset is apparent fishing effort based on transmissions broadcast using the automatic identification system (AIS). Today we receive over 110 million AIS messages each day and continually update our technology and algorithms to improve our ability to monitor global commercial fishing. Using cloud computing, machine learning and public vessel registry information, we analyze tens of millions of AIS positions each day to map global apparent fishing effort. These data are first run through a series of algorithms designed to filter out corrupt or incomplete records and assign additional information to each AIS message, such as the distance from shore, depth and time since the vessel’s previous AIS position. Before we can map fishing activity, we must first identify fishing vessels in the AIS data. When our fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. To generate maps of apparent fishing effort we then “rasterize” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. While AIS provides a revolutionary way to monitor global commercial fishing activity, there are several important limitations and caveats. First, AIS data includes only a small fraction—approximately 100,000—of the world’s estimated 3.3 million fishing vessels. As a result, fewer AIS positions are received by vessels operating in certain parts of the world, limiting the effectiveness of our machine learning models and our ability to detect apparent fishing effort. All users of our map can access our near real-time data to create heat maps to visualize patterns of commercial fishing activity, view tracks of individual vessels and overlay information like the locations of marine protected areas or countries’ exclusive economic zones. Our AIS-based static apparent fishing effort data can be downloaded via our data download portal.
